newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh to try to revive Japan's faith as donor.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh to try to revive Japan's faith as donor.

text.p: Bangladesh, under fire from Japan for its poor utilisation of foreign aid, said on Thursday it would try to revive Tokyo's faith as a donor.

Bangladesh expressed its determination to woo the Japanese government after a visiting team from Tokyo warned on Wednesday that aid would slow unless Dhaka improved efficiency in preparing and implementing projects.
"We appreciate the Japanese concern. We are trying very hard to revive their confidence by resolving the problems," Finance Minister S.A.M.S. Kibria told Reuters.
"The utilisation of Japanese assistance has not made any progress during the last two years," Shuichiro Megata, a senior Japanese government official, told the media on Wednesday.

Megata, who headed a six-member delegation which held consultations with Bangladesh on aid, said Dhaka had been inefficient and slow in preparing project plans and formulating procedures for seeking aid.
Kibria conceded there had been delays in implementing foreign-aided project over the past two years, which government officials attributed to political instability and procedural bottlenecks.
Japan provides Bangladesh with around $300 million in aid and grants annually, but says Dhaka is in most cases unable to offer details of projects or information on their priority.
Finance ministry officials said Japan has offered nearly $4.0 billion since 1971, about half of this total in the form of grants.
Finance ministry officials said Japan was keen to offer more assistance for infrastructure development, particularly in the power sector.
"The country has already financed two power projects with a generation capacity of about 200 megawatts," one official said.
He said Japan was also expected to take a stake in the proposed 300 megawatt Meghna Ghat power project.

The officials said Japan was expected to donate to a $300 million infrastructure fund which aims to promote private sector investment in Bangladesh's energy sector. The World Bank is likely to offer $150 million for the fund, they added.
